Create and pitch one persuasive advertisement for the audience in the client brief.
Understand the audience, choose and shape a product, create the advertisement, practise advertising techniques, choose media space, and present the finished campaign.
Action: Walk to Client Briefing and press Space or Enter.
Why: The pair needs a shared account of the audience situation, need and values before making creative decisions.
Lead role: The Strategist reads the brief aloud and checks the audience purpose.
Partner action: The Art Director identifies visual ideas that could suit that audience.
What each role is responsible for
Art Director: controls visual decisions, including hierarchy, colour, framing, composition, imagery, scale and the final presentation.
On this site, the Art Director leads when the pair edits how the product and advertisement look.
Strategist: controls audience and message decisions, including product value, AIDA, headline, claims, price and media route.
On this site, the Strategist leads when the pair decides what the audience should think, feel or do.

Salience makes one element attract attention before the others.
It gives the audience a clear first reading point.
One large product against smaller supporting details.
Colour creates mood, associations and links between visual elements.
A controlled palette can support the product identity and audience mood.
Repeat one accent colour on related elements.
Contrast makes differences in light, colour, size or shape noticeable.
It separates important information and improves legibility.
Place dark type on a light area, or light type on a dark area.
Leading lines use visible or implied lines to guide the viewer's eye.
They direct attention towards the product or another important element.
Angle an edge, path or repeated shape towards the product.
Framing places visual elements around a subject to define its viewing area.
It isolates the subject and controls where the audience looks.
Use an arch, border or foreground shapes around the product.
Negative space is the deliberately empty area around visual elements.
It reduces crowding and makes the main message easier to notice.
Leave a clear area around the product name or product image.
Depth uses foreground, middle and background layers to create visual distance.
It can make a flat advertisement feel dimensional and organised.
Overlap a foreground shape, the product and a background element.
The rule of odds groups related subjects in an odd number, often three or five.
An odd group can feel balanced without looking rigidly paired.
Use three supporting shapes or three product details as a group.
Juxtaposition places unlike elements together so their difference is clear.
The contrast can create surprise or clarify an idea about the product.
Place an ordinary setting beside one deliberately unexpected product feature.
Typography uses typeface, size, weight, spacing and line breaks to shape written information.
It controls tone, emphasis and legibility without changing the words.
Change size or line breaks to emphasise an existing key word.
Visual hierarchy orders elements so the audience reads them in a planned sequence.
It makes the first, second and final reading points clear.
Use decreasing size and emphasis across the product, support and price.
